title: Transcript
use_cases: Use when designing a campaign map that requires realistic geography and purpose-driven terrain.
Implement when planning a continent split to create distinct northern and southern regions with a central scar.
Configure when adding rivers and lakes that flow logically from mountain ranges to oceans for political boundaries.
Create when drafting map outlines for islands, channels, and inlets to enhance exploration depth.
Plan when integrating magic elements that justify unconventional terrain features within a realistic setting.

Dungeons and Dragons, as well as many other

Well, that's what we're going to talk about today. We're going to talk about maps

And one of the first things that your players will want to see is a map. This gives them a sense of 
the world that they are about to explore. When building your map, there's a few key things that 
you want to keep in mind. First, you want to make sure that it's big enough that players can get 
lost in it, but not so big that it feels empty.
A lot of mistakes that new Dungeon Masters make is 
that they'll make a map and then in their minds, they'll just see it as rolling green hills and 
forests for pretty much the entire map. That's just what they picture, and that's because they 
haven't taken the time to think about what is actually in the world and what the smaller, more 
intricate locations are going to look like.
You also want to fill it with interesting 
locations, right side quests, landmarks, things that are going to make your players want 
to explore every inch of it. You also want to make sure that each location has a purpose, and it's 
fleshed out enough that players can get a sense of what it would be like to visit there and not 
just random things thrown around on the map.
